igcse-0580-surds-exact-roots.description: Recognise a surd, locate it between integers and extract the largest square factor.

sections.title: When is a square root an exact surd?
sections.label: Exact value and size
sections.intro: When the positive integer inside a square root is a perfect square, its root is an integer. If that integer is between two consecutive squares, its square root lies between the corresponding two integers.

blocks.html: A surd is an exact irrational root. In \(3<\sqrt{14}<4\), the middle term gives the value exactly and the outer numbers show its size. A finite calculator display such as \(3.742\) gives an approximation.

figure.alt: A number line from 3 to 4 shows the approximate position of the square root of 14.
figure.caption: The exact root lies between 3 and 4 because 14 lies between 9 and 16. Its placement on the line is approximate.

blocks.title: Distinguish exact square roots
blocks.prompt: One of \(\sqrt{16}\) and \(\sqrt{18}\) is an integer and one is not. Which set contains \(\sqrt{18}\)?
blocks.hint: Check whether the integer under this square root is a perfect square.
blocks.solution:
The neighbouring squares are \(16\) and \(25\).

\(18\) lies strictly between them and is an integer that is not a perfect square.

The square root of a non-square positive integer is irrational. The comparison \(4<\sqrt{18}<5\) locates its value.

retry.feedback: A square root of a positive integer is an integer only when the radicand is a perfect square.

blocks.html: The square root sign denotes the non-negative root. The equation \(x^2=14\) has two solutions, whereas \(\sqrt{14}\) is a single positive number.

blocks.title: Bound an exact square root
blocks.prompt: Find the consecutive integers \(a\) and \(b\) for which \(a<\sqrt{28}
blocks.hint: Find the largest square smaller than the number under the root.
blocks.solution:
Look for square numbers on both sides of \(28\).

\(5^2=25<28<36=6^2\).

Taking the positive square root of each number preserves this order, so the integers are \(5\) and \(6\).

blocks.html: When the question says exact or gives a surd form, leave the radical in the result.

sections.title: How do I take a square factor out?
sections.label: Take out a perfect square
sections.intro: Start with a square that divides the radicand exactly. Divisibility matters because the leftover factor must still be an integer.

blocks.html: Use \(\sqrt{k^2d}=k\sqrt d\) for positive integer \(k\). Choose the largest square factor you can find. You may take out smaller factors one at a time, provided you stop only when none remain.

blocks.title: Take out a square factor
blocks.prompt: Write \(\sqrt{112}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{7}\). Find \(a\).
blocks.hint: Split the radicand into a perfect square times the remaining factor.
blocks.solution:
Look for a perfect square that divides \(112\).

\(112=16\times 7\), so \(\sqrt{112}=\sqrt{16}\times \sqrt{7}\). The first root is \(4\).

The fully simplified result is \(4\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=4\).

blocks.html: For \(\sqrt{63}\), use \(63=9\times 7\). The square root of 9 is 3, so the multiplier outside the root is 3.

blocks.title: Finish an incomplete simplification
blocks.prompt: Write \(2\sqrt{80}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{5}\). Find \(a\).
blocks.hint: Look again inside the root. A square factor may still be there.
blocks.solution:
The original root could come from \(\sqrt{320}\). Taking out \(2\) still leaves \(80\) under the root.

The remaining radicand is \(80=16\times 5\). Taking out this square factor gives \(2\times 4\sqrt{5}\).

The fully simplified result is \(8\sqrt{5}\), so \(a=8\).

blocks.html: Check your simplification by squaring it. The result should be the original radicand.

sections.title: How do I use the same idea for a length?
sections.label: Exact lengths and outside factors
sections.intro: A square with area given has an exact side length equal to the positive square root of that area. Multiplying a length by a scale factor multiplies the entire expression.

blocks.html: If the question gives an outside multiplier already, multiply it by the factor taken out. Leave a square-free radicand in the result.

blocks.title: Multiply the outside coefficients
blocks.prompt: Write \(3\sqrt{48}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\).
blocks.hint: The number already outside the root multiplies the number taken out.
blocks.solution:
Factor the radicand as \(16\times 3\).

Use \(\sqrt{48}=4\sqrt{3}\). The two coefficients multiply to \(3\times 4=12\).

The fully simplified result is \(12\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=12\).

blocks.html: If you double a side length, its square area is multiplied by four. Doubling a number under a root does not double the root.

blocks.title: Find the exact side of a square
blocks.prompt: A square has area \(50\) square centimetres. Write the answer as \(a\sqrt{2}\) cm. Find \(a\).
blocks.hint: Take the square root of the area, then extract a square factor.
blocks.solution:
A square has area equal to its side squared. Its positive side length is \(\sqrt{50}\) cm.

The radicand has the square factor \(25\). The remaining factor is \(2\).

The fully simplified result is \(5\sqrt{2}\) cm, so \(a=5\).

blocks.html: Write the length unit after the full surd expression and the area unit after its square.

examples.title: Distinguish exact square roots
examples.question:
One of \(\sqrt{9}\) and \(\sqrt{10}\) is an integer and one is not. Which set contains \(\sqrt{10}\)?

  1. Integers
  2. Irrational numbers
  3. Non-integer rational numbers
solution: The neighbouring squares are \(9\) and \(16\).
\(10\) lies strictly between them and is an integer that is not a perfect square.
The square root of a non-square positive integer is irrational. The comparison \(3<\sqrt{10}<4\) locates its value.

examples.title: Bound an exact square root
examples.question: Find the consecutive integers \(a\) and \(b\) for which \(a<\sqrt{18}
solution: Look for square numbers on both sides of \(18\).
Taking the positive square root of each number preserves this order, so the integers are \(4\) and \(5\).

examples.title: Take out a square factor
examples.question: Write \(\sqrt{45}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{5}\). Find \(a\).
solution: Look for a perfect square that divides \(45\).
\(45=9\times 5\), so \(\sqrt{45}=\sqrt{9}\times \sqrt{5}\). The first root is \(3\).
The fully simplified result is \(3\sqrt{5}\), so \(a=3\).

examples.title: Finish an incomplete simplification
examples.question: Write \(2\sqrt{27}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\).
solution: The original root could come from \(\sqrt{108}\). Taking out \(2\) still leaves \(27\) under the root.
The remaining radicand is \(27=9\times 3\). Taking out this square factor gives \(2\times 3\sqrt{3}\).
The fully simplified result is \(6\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=6\).

examples.title: Multiply the outside coefficients
examples.question: Write \(2\sqrt{63}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{7}\). Find \(a\).
solution: Factor the radicand as \(9\times 7\).
Use \(\sqrt{63}=3\sqrt{7}\). The two coefficients multiply to \(2\times 3=6\).
The fully simplified result is \(6\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=6\).

solution: A square has area equal to its side squared. Its positive side length is \(\sqrt{48}\) cm.
The radicand has the square factor \(16\). The remaining factor is \(3\).
The fully simplified result is \(4\sqrt{3}\) cm, so \(a=4\).

glossary.definition: The square of an integer.
An irrational root left in exact form.
The number under the root sign.
A positive integer with no square divisor greater than 1.
A value close to the exact value.

revision.body:
Exact value and size

A surd is an exact irrational root. In \(3<\sqrt{14}<4\), the middle term gives the value exactly and the outer numbers show its size. A finite calculator display such as \(3.742\) gives an approximation.

Take out a perfect square

Use \(\sqrt{k^2d}=k\sqrt d\) for positive integer \(k\). Choose the largest square factor you can find. You may take out smaller factors one at a time, provided you stop only when none remain.

Exact lengths and outside factors

If the question gives an outside multiplier already, multiply it by the factor taken out. Leave a square-free radicand in the result.

Example

Since \(175=25\times7\), \(\sqrt{175}=5\sqrt7\). Squaring the last expression returns 175.

Check yourself

  • Find the consecutive integers that bound \(\sqrt{43}\).
  • Simplify \(3\sqrt{98}\).

Answers \(6<\sqrt{43}<7\) and \(21\sqrt2\).
revision.checks:
• The square root sign denotes the non-negative root. The equation \(x^2=14\) has two solutions, whereas \(\sqrt{14}\) is a single positive number.
  • For \(\sqrt{63}\), use \(63=9\times 7\). The square root of 9 is 3, so the multiplier outside the root is 3.
  • If you double a side length, its square area is multiplied by four. Doubling a number under a root does not double the root.
revision.examTip: Write the length unit after the full surd expression and the area unit after its square.

igcse-0580-surds-surds-operations.description: Decide when to collect matching radicals and when to combine two radicands.

sections.title: When can I collect two surds?
sections.label: Add or subtract matching radicals
sections.intro: Identify what the operation does before moving anything under or out of the root. A sum or difference can be collected when the simplified radical parts match.

blocks.html: Think of \(\sqrt5\) as the common factor in \(4\sqrt5+3\sqrt5\). Adding the coefficients gives \(7\sqrt5\). If one root is still unsimplified, simplify it first.

figure.alt: Two equal square tiles show the repeated size A and a separate larger tile shows size B.
figure.caption: Equal tiles can be counted together. Terms with different simplified radicals remain separate when added.

blocks.title: Collect like surds
blocks.prompt: Write \(\sqrt{252}+\sqrt{28}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{7}\). Find \(a\).
blocks.hint: Separate the square factor in each term. Keep the common square root when combining.
blocks.solution:
Simplify each term first. \(\sqrt{252}=6\sqrt{7}\) and \(\sqrt{28}=2\sqrt{7}\).

The radicals now match. Use the coefficient calculation \(6+2=8\) and keep the radical.

The fully simplified result is \(8\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=8\).

blocks.html: Subtract the outside coefficient and preserve the radicand. Never subtract the radicands because the two terms are joined by subtraction.

blocks.title: Subtract after simplifying
blocks.prompt: Write \(\sqrt{252}-\sqrt{28}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{7}\). Find \(a\).
blocks.hint: Separate the square factor in each term. Keep the common square root when combining.
blocks.solution:
Simplify each term first. \(\sqrt{252}=6\sqrt{7}\) and \(\sqrt{28}=2\sqrt{7}\).

The radicals now match. Use the coefficient calculation \(6-2=4\) and keep the radical.

The fully simplified result is \(4\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=4\).

blocks.html: Leave two terms in an exact answer when the simplified radicals are different.

sections.title: What changes if the operation is multiplication?
sections.label: Unlike radicals and products
sections.intro: The simplification test comes first. If the square-free radicands differ, the sum stays as separate terms. A product follows a different rule.

blocks.html: For non-negative radicands \(a,b\), use \(\sqrt a\sqrt b=\sqrt{ab}\). Any coefficients outside the roots also multiply. Simplify the resulting root if it has a square factor.

blocks.title: Recognise unlike radicals
blocks.prompt: Choose the fully simplified form of \(\sqrt{18}+\sqrt{80}\).
blocks.hint: Simplify both radicals before deciding whether they can be collected.
blocks.solution:
The first square factor is \(9\) and the second is \(16\).

The simplified terms are \(3\sqrt{2}\) and \(4\sqrt{5}\).

The square-free radicands differ, so leave the exact sum as \(3\sqrt{2}+4\sqrt{5}\).

retry.feedback: The rule for joining radicands applies to a product of square roots. Here the operation is addition.

blocks.html: The radical multiplication rule cannot be used for addition. For example, \(\sqrt2+\sqrt3\ne\sqrt5\).

blocks.title: Multiply different square roots
blocks.prompt: Write \(\sqrt{27}\times \sqrt{21}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{7}\). Find \(a\).
blocks.hint: Multiply the two radicands. Then look for the square factor in their product.
blocks.solution:
A product of non-negative square roots can be grouped into one positive square root.

Here the product of the radicands is \(27\times 21=81\times 7\). Extract the square factor.

The fully simplified result is \(9\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=9\).

blocks.html: Before writing a new root, check whether the sign between terms is a multiplication sign or an addition sign.

sections.title: How do I divide or square exact roots?
sections.label: Quotients and squares
sections.intro: The quotient can be put under a single radical with a strictly positive denominator. Squaring a single surd term multiplies it by itself.

blocks.html: For \(a\geq0,\ b>0\), \(\frac{\sqrt a}{\sqrt b}=\sqrt{\frac ab}\). The square of \(k\sqrt d\) is \(k^2d\).

blocks.title: Divide two square roots
blocks.prompt: Write \(\frac{\sqrt{180}}{\sqrt{4}}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{5}\). Find \(a\).
blocks.hint: Divide the radicands before simplifying the remaining root.
blocks.solution:
The denominator is positive. Divide inside one radical to give \(\sqrt{45}\).

The simplified radicand still has square factor \(9\). Extract it to find the coefficient.

The fully simplified result is \(3\sqrt{5}\), so \(a=3\).

blocks.html: Squaring a product squares both factors. A square with side \(4\sqrt3\) has area \(16\times3=48\), not 12.

blocks.title: Square an exact length to find area
blocks.prompt: A square has side length \(4\sqrt{3}\) cm. Find its exact area in square centimetres.
blocks.hint: Square both the outside coefficient and the radical.
blocks.solution:
Square the entire length, including the coefficient \(4\).

\(\left(4\sqrt{3}\right)^2=16\times 3\). The area is \(48\) square centimetres.

blocks.html: Cancel common factors before multiplying large numbers. Keep area and length units distinct.

examples.title: Collect like surds
examples.question: Write \(\sqrt{150}+\sqrt{24}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{6}\). Find \(a\).
solution: Simplify each term first. \(\sqrt{150}=5\sqrt{6}\) and \(\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt{6}\).
The radicals now match. Use the coefficient calculation \(5+2=7\) and keep the radical.
The fully simplified result is \(7\sqrt{6}\), so \(a=7\).

examples.title: Subtract after simplifying
examples.question: Write \(\sqrt{150}-\sqrt{24}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{6}\). Find \(a\).
solution: Simplify each term first. \(\sqrt{150}=5\sqrt{6}\) and \(\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt{6}\).
The radicals now match. Use the coefficient calculation \(5-2=3\) and keep the radical.
The fully simplified result is \(3\sqrt{6}\), so \(a=3\).

examples.title: Recognise unlike radicals
examples.question:
Choose the fully simplified form of \(\sqrt{12}+\sqrt{63}\).

  1. \(2\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt{7}\)
  2. \(\sqrt{75}\)
  3. \(5\sqrt{3}\)
  4. \(2\sqrt{7}+3\sqrt{3}\)
solution: The first square factor is \(4\) and the second is \(9\).
The simplified terms are \(2\sqrt{3}\) and \(3\sqrt{7}\).
The square-free radicands differ, so leave the exact sum as \(2\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt{7}\).

examples.title: Multiply different square roots
examples.question: Write \(\sqrt{8}\times \sqrt{10}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{5}\). Find \(a\).
solution: A product of non-negative square roots can be grouped into one positive square root.
Here the product of the radicands is \(8\times 10=16\times 5\). Extract the square factor.
The fully simplified result is \(4\sqrt{5}\), so \(a=4\).

examples.title: Divide two square roots
examples.question: Write \(\frac{\sqrt{84}}{\sqrt{3}}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{7}\). Find \(a\).
solution: The denominator is positive. Divide inside one radical to give \(\sqrt{28}\).
The simplified radicand still has square factor \(4\). Extract it to find the coefficient.
The fully simplified result is \(2\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=2\).

examples.title: Square an exact length to find area
examples.question: A square has side length \(3\sqrt{7}\) cm. Find its exact area in square centimetres.
solution: Square the entire length, including the coefficient \(3\).
\(\left(3\sqrt{7}\right)^2=9\times 7\). The area is \(63\) square centimetres.

extraPractice.title: Collect like surds
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\sqrt{147}+\sqrt{27}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\).
extraPractice.hint: Separate the square factor in each term. Keep the common square root when combining.
extraPractice.solution:
Simplify each term first. \(\sqrt{147}=7\sqrt{3}\) and \(\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3}\).

The radicals now match. Use the coefficient calculation \(7+3=10\) and keep the radical.

The fully simplified result is \(10\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=10\).

extraPractice.title: Subtract after simplifying
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\sqrt{147}-\sqrt{27}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\).
extraPractice.hint: Separate the square factor in each term. Keep the common square root when combining.
extraPractice.solution:
Simplify each term first. \(\sqrt{147}=7\sqrt{3}\) and \(\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3}\).

The radicals now match. Use the coefficient calculation \(7-3=4\) and keep the radical.

The fully simplified result is \(4\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=4\).

extraPractice.title: Recognise unlike radicals
extraPractice.prompt: Choose the fully simplified form of \(\sqrt{96}+\sqrt{275}\).
extraPractice.hint: Simplify both radicals before deciding whether they can be collected.
extraPractice.solution:
The first square factor is \(16\) and the second is \(25\).

The simplified terms are \(4\sqrt{6}\) and \(5\sqrt{11}\).

The square-free radicands differ, so leave the exact sum as \(4\sqrt{6}+5\sqrt{11}\).

retry.feedback: The rule for joining radicands applies to a product of square roots. Here the operation is addition.

extraPractice.title: Multiply different square roots
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\sqrt{64}\times \sqrt{8}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{2}\). Find \(a\).
extraPractice.hint: Multiply the two radicands. Then look for the square factor in their product.
extraPractice.solution:
A product of non-negative square roots can be grouped into one positive square root.

Here the product of the radicands is \(64\times 8=256\times 2\). Extract the square factor.

The fully simplified result is \(16\sqrt{2}\), so \(a=16\).

extraPractice.title: Divide two square roots
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\frac{\sqrt{240}}{\sqrt{5}}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\).
extraPractice.hint: Divide the radicands before simplifying the remaining root.
extraPractice.solution:
The denominator is positive. Divide inside one radical to give \(\sqrt{48}\).

The simplified radicand still has square factor \(16\). Extract it to find the coefficient.

The fully simplified result is \(4\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=4\).

extraPractice.title: Square an exact length to find area
extraPractice.prompt: A square has side length \(5\sqrt{11}\) cm. Find its exact area in square centimetres.
extraPractice.hint: Square both the outside coefficient and the radical.
extraPractice.solution:
Square the entire length, including the coefficient \(5\).

\(\left(5\sqrt{11}\right)^2=25\times 11\). The area is \(275\) square centimetres.

glossary.definition: Terms with the same radical after simplification.
The multiplier in front of a term.
The result of one quantity divided by another.
A number or expression multiplied by another.
Greater than or equal to zero.

revision.body:
Add or subtract matching radicals

Think of \(\sqrt5\) as the common factor in \(4\sqrt5+3\sqrt5\). Adding the coefficients gives \(7\sqrt5\). If one root is still unsimplified, simplify it first.

Unlike radicals and products

For non-negative radicands \(a,b\), use \(\sqrt a\sqrt b=\sqrt{ab}\). Any coefficients outside the roots also multiply. Simplify the resulting root if it has a square factor.

Quotients and squares

For \(a\geq0,\ b>0\), \(\frac{\sqrt a}{\sqrt b}=\sqrt{\frac ab}\). The square of \(k\sqrt d\) is \(k^2d\).

Example

Simplify \(\sqrt{108}-\sqrt{27}\) to \(6\sqrt3-3\sqrt3=3\sqrt3\).

Check yourself

  • Simplify \(\sqrt{32}+\sqrt{50}\).
  • Work out \(\sqrt{18}\times\sqrt{10}\) in simplest form.

Answers \(9\sqrt2\) and \(6\sqrt5\).
revision.checks:
• Subtract the outside coefficient and preserve the radicand. Never subtract the radicands because the two terms are joined by subtraction.
  • The radical multiplication rule cannot be used for addition. For example, \(\sqrt2+\sqrt3\ne\sqrt5\).
  • Squaring a product squares both factors. A square with side \(4\sqrt3\) has area \(16\times3=48\), not 12.

igcse-0580-surds-surds-brackets.description: Write every product in a bracket expansion, then collect rational and irrational terms.

sections.title: How do I distribute a surd across a bracket?
sections.label: Multiply every term
sections.intro: The same distributive rule works for rational numbers and surds. Start by showing explicitly which two terms the outside factor multiplies.

blocks.html: The product of one surd and an integer usually stays as a surd. A pair of matching square roots multiplies to an integer. Write these contributions as separate terms.

figure.alt: A rectangle is divided into four regions by splitting each of its two side lengths.
figure.caption: Each region uses a different pair of side segments. All four products contribute to the area.

blocks.title: Expand one surd across a bracket
blocks.prompt: Write \(3\sqrt{3}\left(4+2\sqrt{3}\right)\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: The outside factor multiplies both terms. A square root times itself gives its radicand.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the outside surd by both terms inside the bracket.

The two products are \(12\sqrt{3}\) and \(6\times 3\). The second product is rational because the two roots match.

The resulting expression is \(18+12\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=18\) and \(b=12\).

blocks.html: Stopping after multiplying the first term leaves out part of the bracket. Count how many terms were inside it.

blocks.title: Expand two brackets with surds
blocks.prompt: Write \(\left(4+2\sqrt{5}\right)\left(3+3\sqrt{5}\right)\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{5}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: Use four products. Two contribute integers and two contribute surds.
blocks.solution:
Distribute both terms from each bracket to get four products.

Collect the rational terms \(12+30=42\) and the surd coefficients \(12+6=18\).

The resulting expression is \(42+18\sqrt{5}\), so \(a=42\) and \(b=18\).

blocks.html: When the required form is \(a+b\sqrt d\), keep the integer part and radical part distinct.

sections.title: How do I keep track of all four products?
sections.label: Signed products and squares
sections.intro: Each term of the first bracket multiplies each term of the second. For a square, both brackets are identical, so the middle terms match rather than cancel.

blocks.html: Set out four products in a line or grid. First collect the rational products, then collect the signed coefficients of the matching radicals.

blocks.title: Track negative terms in an expansion
blocks.prompt: Write \(\left(3-3\sqrt{3}\right)\left(5+2\sqrt{3}\right)\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: Keep the signs on all four products before collecting like terms.
blocks.solution:
The product of the two rational terms is \(15\). The product of the two surd terms is \(-18\).

The middle terms are \(6\sqrt{3}\) and \(-15\sqrt{3}\). Combine their signed coefficients.

The resulting expression is \(-3-9\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=-3\) and \(b=-9\).

blocks.html: Squaring a difference still gives a positive square of the second term. The middle terms of an expansion like \((a-b)^2\) are both negative.

blocks.title: Square a two-term expression
blocks.prompt: Write \(\left(4-3\sqrt{11}\right)^2\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{11}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: Squaring the two terms separately misses two copies of the cross term.
blocks.solution:
Write the square as a product of two identical brackets. Both cross terms are \(-12\sqrt{11}\).

The endpoint terms give \(4^2+3^2\times 11=115\). Together the cross terms give \(-24\sqrt{11}\).

The resulting expression is \(115-24\sqrt{11}\), so \(a=115\) and \(b=-24\).

blocks.html: Simplify the surds in each bracket first if the question uses different radicands with a common square-free part.

sections.title: When do the cross terms cancel?
sections.label: Difference of two squares and area
sections.intro: When the brackets have the same terms with opposite signs between them, one cross product is the negative of the other.

blocks.html: Use \((u+v)(u-v)=u^2-v^2\) only after checking for those opposite signs. For a rectangular area, use the full length times the full width.

blocks.title: Spot a difference of two squares
blocks.prompt: Work out the exact value of \(\left(8+3\sqrt{7}\right)\left(8-3\sqrt{7}\right)\).
blocks.hint: The brackets have the same two terms with opposite signs between them.
blocks.solution:
The two brackets have matching rational parts. Their radical terms have opposite signs.

The cross terms cancel. The rational result is \(8^2-3^2\times 7=1\).

blocks.html: The result of multiplying opposite-sign brackets can be negative. Check the order of the two squares instead of taking their absolute difference.

blocks.title: Expand to find an exact area
blocks.prompt: A rectangle has sides \(5+2\sqrt{11}\) cm and \(3\sqrt{11}\) cm. Write its area in square centimetres in the form \(a+b\sqrt{11}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: The shorter side multiplies the whole longer side.
blocks.solution:
Multiply length by width to find the area in square centimetres.

The products are \(15\sqrt{11}\) and \(6\times 11\). Add the rational and surd parts.

The resulting expression is \(66+15\sqrt{11}\), so \(a=66\) and \(b=15\).

blocks.html: Show the separate contributions before giving the exact area or coefficient. Use square units for area.

examples.title: Expand one surd across a bracket
examples.question: Write \(2\sqrt{5}\left(3+\sqrt{5}\right)\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{5}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
solution: Multiply the outside surd by both terms inside the bracket.
The two products are \(6\sqrt{5}\) and \(2\times 5\). The second product is rational because the two roots match.
The resulting expression is \(10+6\sqrt{5}\), so \(a=10\) and \(b=6\).

examples.title: Expand two brackets with surds
examples.question: Write \(\left(3+\sqrt{7}\right)\left(2+2\sqrt{7}\right)\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{7}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
solution: Distribute both terms from each bracket to get four products.
Collect the rational terms \(6+14=20\) and the surd coefficients \(6+2=8\).
The resulting expression is \(20+8\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=20\) and \(b=8\).

examples.title: Track negative terms in an expansion
examples.question: Write \(\left(2-2\sqrt{6}\right)\left(4+\sqrt{6}\right)\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{6}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
solution: The product of the two rational terms is \(8\). The product of the two surd terms is \(-12\).
The middle terms are \(2\sqrt{6}\) and \(-8\sqrt{6}\). Combine their signed coefficients.
The resulting expression is \(-4-6\sqrt{6}\), so \(a=-4\) and \(b=-6\).

examples.title: Square a two-term expression
examples.question: Write \(\left(3-2\sqrt{3}\right)^2\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
solution: Write the square as a product of two identical brackets. Both cross terms are \(-6\sqrt{3}\).
The endpoint terms give \(3^2+2^2\times 3=21\). Together the cross terms give \(-12\sqrt{3}\).
The resulting expression is \(21-12\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=21\) and \(b=-12\).

examples.title: Spot a difference of two squares
examples.question: Work out the exact value of \(\left(7+2\sqrt{5}\right)\left(7-2\sqrt{5}\right)\).
solution: The two brackets have matching rational parts. Their radical terms have opposite signs.
The cross terms cancel. The rational result is \(7^2-2^2\times 5=29\).

examples.title: Expand to find an exact area
examples.question: A rectangle has sides \(4+\sqrt{5}\) cm and \(2\sqrt{5}\) cm. Write its area in square centimetres in the form \(a+b\sqrt{5}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
solution: Multiply length by width to find the area in square centimetres.
The products are \(8\sqrt{5}\) and \(2\times 5\). Add the rational and surd parts.
The resulting expression is \(10+8\sqrt{5}\), so \(a=10\) and \(b=8\).

extraPractice.title: Expand one surd across a bracket
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(4\sqrt{7}\left(5+3\sqrt{7}\right)\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{7}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
extraPractice.hint: The outside factor multiplies both terms. A square root times itself gives its radicand.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiply the outside surd by both terms inside the bracket.

The two products are \(20\sqrt{7}\) and \(12\times 7\). The second product is rational because the two roots match.

The resulting expression is \(84+20\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=84\) and \(b=20\).

extraPractice.title: Expand two brackets with surds
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\left(5+3\sqrt{3}\right)\left(4+4\sqrt{3}\right)\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
extraPractice.hint: Use four products. Two contribute integers and two contribute surds.
extraPractice.solution:
Distribute both terms from each bracket to get four products.

Collect the rational terms \(20+36=56\) and the surd coefficients \(20+12=32\).

The resulting expression is \(56+32\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=56\) and \(b=32\).

extraPractice.title: Track negative terms in an expansion
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\left(4-4\sqrt{11}\right)\left(6+3\sqrt{11}\right)\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{11}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
extraPractice.hint: Keep the signs on all four products before collecting like terms.
extraPractice.solution:
The product of the two rational terms is \(24\). The product of the two surd terms is \(-132\).

The middle terms are \(12\sqrt{11}\) and \(-24\sqrt{11}\). Combine their signed coefficients.

The resulting expression is \(-108-12\sqrt{11}\), so \(a=-108\) and \(b=-12\).

extraPractice.title: Square a two-term expression
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\left(5-4\sqrt{7}\right)^2\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{7}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
extraPractice.hint: Squaring the two terms separately misses two copies of the cross term.
extraPractice.solution:
Write the square as a product of two identical brackets. Both cross terms are \(-20\sqrt{7}\).

The endpoint terms give \(5^2+4^2\times 7=137\). Together the cross terms give \(-40\sqrt{7}\).

The resulting expression is \(137-40\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=137\) and \(b=-40\).

extraPractice.title: Spot a difference of two squares
extraPractice.prompt: Work out the exact value of \(\left(9+4\sqrt{2}\right)\left(9-4\sqrt{2}\right)\).
extraPractice.hint: The brackets have the same two terms with opposite signs between them.
extraPractice.solution:
The two brackets have matching rational parts. Their radical terms have opposite signs.

The cross terms cancel. The rational result is \(9^2-4^2\times 2=49\).

extraPractice.title: Expand to find an exact area
extraPractice.prompt: A rectangle has sides \(6+3\sqrt{3}\) cm and \(4\sqrt{3}\) cm. Write its area in square centimetres in the form \(a+b\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
extraPractice.hint: The shorter side multiplies the whole longer side.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiply length by width to find the area in square centimetres.

The products are \(24\sqrt{3}\) and \(12\times 3\). Add the rational and surd parts.

The resulting expression is \(36+24\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=36\) and \(b=24\).

glossary.definition: Multiply each term in a sum by the outside factor.
Products using one rational and one radical term in a two-bracket expansion.
The part that can be written as a ratio of integers.
A product of a sum and its related difference.
An equivalent expression with the brackets multiplied out.

revision.body:
Multiply every term

The product of one surd and an integer usually stays as a surd. A pair of matching square roots multiplies to an integer. Write these contributions as separate terms.

Signed products and squares

Set out four products in a line or grid. First collect the rational products, then collect the signed coefficients of the matching radicals.

Difference of two squares and area

Use \((u+v)(u-v)=u^2-v^2\) only after checking for those opposite signs. For a rectangular area, use the full length times the full width.

Example

In \((4-\sqrt7)^2\), the middle terms give \(-8\sqrt7\) and the endpoint terms give \(16+7=23\).

Check yourself

  • Expand \(2\sqrt3(4-\sqrt3)\).
  • Work out \((5+2\sqrt7)(5-2\sqrt7)\).

Answers \(-6+8\sqrt3\) and \(-3\).
revision.checks:
• Stopping after multiplying the first term leaves out part of the bracket. Count how many terms were inside it.
  • Squaring a difference still gives a positive square of the second term. The middle terms of an expansion like \((a-b)^2\) are both negative.
  • The result of multiplying opposite-sign brackets can be negative. Check the order of the two squares instead of taking their absolute difference.
revision.examTip: Show the separate contributions before giving the exact area or coefficient. Use square units for area.

igcse-0580-surds-single-denominators.description: Use a factor equal to one to clear a radical from a denominator and reduce the fraction.

sections.title: How do I change the form without changing the value?
sections.label: Find a multiplier equal to one
sections.intro: Rationalising a denominator means rewriting the same value with a rational number at the bottom. The numerator may still contain a surd.

blocks.html: If the denominator is \(\sqrt d\), multiply both parts of the fraction by \(\sqrt d\). The common multiplier is nonzero. The denominator now contains \(\sqrt d\times\sqrt d=d\).

blocks.title: Rationalise a single square root
blocks.prompt: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{4}{\sqrt{11}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{11}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: Use one copy of the square root at the top and another at the bottom. Then reduce the numerical fraction.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{11}\). The fraction made from two copies of that root is 1.

The unreduced rationalised result is \(\frac{4\sqrt{11}}{11}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{4}{11}=\frac{4}{11}\). The simplified expression is \(\frac{4\sqrt{11}}{11}\).

blocks.html: Multiplying only the bottom changes the value. The whole fraction must be multiplied by a fraction equal to one.

blocks.title: Reduce after rationalising
blocks.prompt: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{9}{\sqrt{3}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{3}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: Use one copy of the square root at the top and another at the bottom. Then reduce the numerical fraction.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{3}\). The fraction made from two copies of that root is 1.

The unreduced rationalised result is \(\frac{9\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{9}{3}=\frac{3}{1}\). The simplified expression is \(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{1}\).

blocks.html: Show the multiplier on both parts of the fraction. Reduce any common numerical factor afterwards.

sections.title: How do I handle a coefficient or a square factor?
sections.label: Rationalise then reduce
sections.intro: When the denominator is a multiple of a root, only the radical factor needs another copy of itself. Simplify a radicand with square factors before choosing the multiplier.

blocks.html: In \(\frac{3}{2\sqrt7}\), multiplying by \(\frac{\sqrt7}{\sqrt7}\) produces a denominator of \(14\). In a root of a fraction, splitting the roots can reveal an ordinary surd denominator.

blocks.title: Rationalise a multiple of a square root
blocks.prompt: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{4}{3\sqrt{11}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{11}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: Use one copy of the square root at the top and another at the bottom. Then reduce the numerical fraction.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{11}\). The fraction made from two copies of that root is 1.

The unreduced rationalised result is \(\frac{4\sqrt{11}}{33}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{4}{33}=\frac{4}{33}\). The simplified expression is \(\frac{4\sqrt{11}}{33}\).

blocks.html: The root in the denominator may simplify first. Rationalising a larger expression immediately can leave an unnecessarily complicated fraction.

blocks.title: Rationalise a root of a fraction
blocks.prompt: Write \(\sqrt{\frac{9}{80}}\) as \(\frac{a\sqrt{5}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: Separate the roots first and simplify the denominator, then make the denominator rational.
blocks.solution:
Split the root across the fraction. \(\sqrt{\frac{9}{80}}=\frac{3}{4\sqrt{5}}\).

Multiply both the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{5}\). This gives \(\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{20}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{3}{20}=\frac{3}{20}\) to obtain \(\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{20}\).

blocks.html: If a final coefficient is a fraction, write it in lowest terms. Treat coefficient and radicand as different parts of the answer.

sections.title: When can I cancel instead of multiplying?
sections.label: Remove a common factor directly
sections.intro: Check whether the same root is already a factor of the entire numerator and the entire denominator. If it is, cancelling that nonzero common factor makes the denominator rational.

blocks.html: For \(\frac{6\sqrt5}{8\sqrt5}\), first cancel \(\sqrt5\), then reduce \(\frac68\) to \(\frac34\).

blocks.title: Simplify a radical before rationalising
blocks.prompt: Write \(\frac{3}{\sqrt{80}}\) as \(\frac{a\sqrt{5}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: Separate the roots first and simplify the denominator, then make the denominator rational.
blocks.solution:
Take the square factor out of the denominator to give \(\frac{3}{4\sqrt{5}}\).

Multiply both the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{5}\). This gives \(\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{20}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{3}{20}=\frac{3}{20}\) to obtain \(\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{20}\).

blocks.html: Cancellation only removes common factors. The term \(\sqrt5\) cannot be cancelled from the sum \(6+\sqrt5\).

blocks.title: Recognise cancellation of a common surd
blocks.prompt: Write \(\frac{3\sqrt{11}}{4\sqrt{11}}\) as \(\frac{p}{q}\) with coprime positive integers \(p\) and \(q\). Find \(p\) and \(q\).
blocks.hint: Check for a common multiplicative factor before looking for a rationalising multiplier.
blocks.solution:
The positive factor \(\sqrt{11}\) appears at the top and bottom.

Cancel that nonzero common factor to leave \(\frac{3}{4}\), which reduces to \(\frac{3}{4}\).

blocks.html: In a written answer, show the factor that cancels and the final reduced denominator.

examples.title: Rationalise a single square root
examples.question: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{3}{\sqrt{7}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{7}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
solution: Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{7}\). The fraction made from two copies of that root is 1.
The unreduced rationalised result is \(\frac{3\sqrt{7}}{7}\).
Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{3}{7}=\frac{3}{7}\). The simplified expression is \(\frac{3\sqrt{7}}{7}\).

examples.title: Reduce after rationalising
examples.question: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{10}{\sqrt{5}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{5}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
solution: Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{5}\). The fraction made from two copies of that root is 1.
The unreduced rationalised result is \(\frac{10\sqrt{5}}{5}\).
Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{10}{5}=\frac{2}{1}\). The simplified expression is \(\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{1}\).

examples.title: Rationalise a multiple of a square root
examples.question: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{3}{2\sqrt{6}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{6}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
solution: Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{6}\). The fraction made from two copies of that root is 1.
The unreduced rationalised result is \(\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{12}\).
Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{3}{12}=\frac{1}{4}\). The simplified expression is \(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}\).

examples.title: Rationalise a root of a fraction
examples.question: Write \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{18}}\) as \(\frac{a\sqrt{2}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
solution: Split the root across the fraction. \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{18}}=\frac{2}{3\sqrt{2}}\).
Multiply both the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{2}\). This gives \(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{6}\).
Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}\) to obtain \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\).

examples.title: Simplify a radical before rationalising
examples.question: Write \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{27}}\) as \(\frac{a\sqrt{3}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
solution: Take the square factor out of the denominator to give \(\frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}\).
Multiply both the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{3}\). This gives \(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}\).
Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{2}{9}=\frac{2}{9}\) to obtain \(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}\).

examples.title: Recognise cancellation of a common surd
examples.question: Write \(\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3\sqrt{5}}\) as \(\frac{p}{q}\) with coprime positive integers \(p\) and \(q\). Find \(p\) and \(q\).
solution: The positive factor \(\sqrt{5}\) appears at the top and bottom.
Cancel that nonzero common factor to leave \(\frac{2}{3}\), which reduces to \(\frac{2}{3}\).

extraPractice.title: Rationalise a single square root
extraPractice.prompt: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{5}{\sqrt{13}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{13}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
extraPractice.hint: Use one copy of the square root at the top and another at the bottom. Then reduce the numerical fraction.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{13}\). The fraction made from two copies of that root is 1.

The unreduced rationalised result is \(\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{13}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{5}{13}=\frac{5}{13}\). The simplified expression is \(\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{13}\).

extraPractice.title: Reduce after rationalising
extraPractice.prompt: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{28}{\sqrt{7}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{7}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
extraPractice.hint: Use one copy of the square root at the top and another at the bottom. Then reduce the numerical fraction.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{7}\). The fraction made from two copies of that root is 1.

The unreduced rationalised result is \(\frac{28\sqrt{7}}{7}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{28}{7}=\frac{4}{1}\). The simplified expression is \(\frac{4\sqrt{7}}{1}\).

extraPractice.title: Rationalise a multiple of a square root
extraPractice.prompt: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{5}{4\sqrt{5}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{5}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
extraPractice.hint: Use one copy of the square root at the top and another at the bottom. Then reduce the numerical fraction.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{5}\). The fraction made from two copies of that root is 1.

The unreduced rationalised result is \(\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{20}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{5}{20}=\frac{1}{4}\). The simplified expression is \(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}\).

extraPractice.title: Rationalise a root of a fraction
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\sqrt{\frac{16}{275}}\) as \(\frac{a\sqrt{11}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
extraPractice.hint: Separate the roots first and simplify the denominator, then make the denominator rational.
extraPractice.solution:
Split the root across the fraction. \(\sqrt{\frac{16}{275}}=\frac{4}{5\sqrt{11}}\).

Multiply both the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{11}\). This gives \(\frac{4\sqrt{11}}{55}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{4}{55}=\frac{4}{55}\) to obtain \(\frac{4\sqrt{11}}{55}\).

extraPractice.title: Simplify a radical before rationalising
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\frac{4}{\sqrt{175}}\) as \(\frac{a\sqrt{7}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
extraPractice.hint: Separate the roots first and simplify the denominator, then make the denominator rational.
extraPractice.solution:
Take the square factor out of the denominator to give \(\frac{4}{5\sqrt{7}}\).

Multiply both the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{7}\). This gives \(\frac{4\sqrt{7}}{35}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{4}{35}=\frac{4}{35}\) to obtain \(\frac{4\sqrt{7}}{35}\).

extraPractice.title: Recognise cancellation of a common surd
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\frac{4\sqrt{7}}{5\sqrt{7}}\) as \(\frac{p}{q}\) with coprime positive integers \(p\) and \(q\). Find \(p\) and \(q\).
extraPractice.hint: Check for a common multiplicative factor before looking for a rationalising multiplier.
extraPractice.solution:
The positive factor \(\sqrt{7}\) appears at the top and bottom.

Cancel that nonzero common factor to leave \(\frac{4}{5}\), which reduces to \(\frac{4}{5}\).

glossary.definition: Rewrite a fraction with a rational denominator without changing its value.
The top expression in a fraction.
The nonzero expression below the fraction bar.
Having no common positive integer factor greater than 1.
Divide the numerator and denominator by the same nonzero factor.

revision.body:
Find a multiplier equal to one

If the denominator is \(\sqrt d\), multiply both parts of the fraction by \(\sqrt d\). The common multiplier is nonzero. The denominator now contains \(\sqrt d\times\sqrt d=d\).

Rationalise then reduce

In \(\frac{3}{2\sqrt7}\), multiplying by \(\frac{\sqrt7}{\sqrt7}\) produces a denominator of \(14\). In a root of a fraction, splitting the roots can reveal an ordinary surd denominator.

Remove a common factor directly

For \(\frac{6\sqrt5}{8\sqrt5}\), first cancel \(\sqrt5\), then reduce \(\frac68\) to \(\frac34\).

Example

For \(\frac{4}{3\sqrt2}\), multiply top and bottom by \(\sqrt2\) to get \(\frac{4\sqrt2}{6}=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}\).

Check yourself

  • Rationalise \(\frac5{\sqrt{14}}\).
  • Reduce \(\frac{15\sqrt7}{9\sqrt7}\) to a rational number.

Answers \(\frac{5\sqrt{14}}{14}\) and \(\frac53\).
revision.checks:
• Multiplying only the bottom changes the value. The whole fraction must be multiplied by a fraction equal to one.
  • The root in the denominator may simplify first. Rationalising a larger expression immediately can leave an unnecessarily complicated fraction.
  • Cancellation only removes common factors. The term \(\sqrt5\) cannot be cancelled from the sum \(6+\sqrt5\).
revision.examTip: In a written answer, show the factor that cancels and the final reduced denominator.

igcse-0580-surds-conjugates.description: Use the matching sign change to eliminate a surd from a two-term denominator and solve mixed problems.

sections.title: Which multiplier clears a two-term denominator?
sections.label: Use the conjugate
sections.intro: A denominator with two terms needs a whole bracket as its multiplier. Find the bracket with the same two pieces but the opposite sign on the radical term.

blocks.html: For \(a+b\sqrt d\), use \(a-b\sqrt d\). The cross terms cancel, and the denominator becomes \(a^2-b^2d\). Multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate preserves the exact value.

figure.alt: A signed product grid has two side contributions of opposite signs and shows that they cancel.
figure.caption: In the product of conjugates, the two cross terms are equal in size and have opposite signs.

blocks.title: Choose a rationalising multiplier
blocks.prompt: Which multiplier makes \(5+3\sqrt{5}\) rational when used in a product?
blocks.hint: Look for the bracket that gives a difference of two squares.
blocks.solution:
The product must have no surviving radical component. Use the bracket with the same rational part and the opposite radical part.

Multiplying by \(5-3\sqrt{5}\) gives \(5^2-9\times 5=-20\).

blocks.html: Multiplying by the root alone usually leaves a radical from the rational term. It cannot clear both terms.

blocks.title: Get an integer pair after rationalising
blocks.prompt: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{14}{5-\sqrt{11}}\). Give the two integers \(a\) and \(b\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{11}\).
blocks.hint: Change the sign between the terms, then use that entire new bracket at the top and the bottom.
blocks.solution:
Use \(5+\sqrt{11}\) as the common multiplier. Its radical term has the opposite sign.

The bottom becomes \(5^2-1\times 11=14\) after the cross terms cancel.

The top becomes \(70+14\sqrt{11}\). Simplify the signs and common factors to obtain \(5+\sqrt{11}\).

blocks.html: Copy the whole conjugate into both parts of the multiplying fraction.

sections.title: How do I reduce a rationalised result?
sections.label: Handle signs and reduce a common factor
sections.intro: After rationalising, expand the numerator if the question asks for a coefficient form. The result at the bottom is a nonzero rational number.

blocks.html: If the denominator is negative, move the negative sign through the entire numerator. Divide all integer coefficients and the denominator by their common factor before reading the requested values.

blocks.title: Use a conjugate when the radical already has a coefficient
blocks.prompt: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{18}{9+3\sqrt{7}}\). Give the two integers \(a\) and \(b\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{7}\).
blocks.hint: Change the sign between the terms, then use that entire new bracket at the top and the bottom.
blocks.solution:
Use \(9-3\sqrt{7}\) as the common multiplier. Its radical term has the opposite sign.

The bottom becomes \(9^2-9\times 7=18\) after the cross terms cancel.

The top becomes \(162-54\sqrt{7}\). Simplify the signs and common factors to obtain \(9-3\sqrt{7}\).

blocks.html: In \(\frac{4-2\sqrt3}{-6}\), changing the denominator to 6 also changes both signs in the numerator. Cancelling requires a factor shared by both numerator terms and the denominator.

blocks.title: Make the final denominator positive
blocks.prompt: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{3}{2-2\sqrt{17}}\). Give \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) in the form \(\frac{a+b\sqrt{17}}{c}\). Use integers with \(c>0\) and no common factor greater than 1.
blocks.hint: Change the sign between the terms, then use that entire new bracket at the top and the bottom.
blocks.solution:
Use \(2+2\sqrt{17}\) as the common multiplier. Its radical term has the opposite sign.

The bottom becomes \(2^2-4\times 17=-64\) after the cross terms cancel.

The top becomes \(6+6\sqrt{17}\). Simplify the signs and common factors to obtain \(\frac{-3-3\sqrt{17}}{32}\).

sections.title: How do I choose a route in a mixed problem?
sections.label: Choose the first useful step
sections.intro: Look at each term separately. A root with a square factor can be simplified first. A fraction with a radical denominator can be rationalised first. Combine matching radicals after those steps.

blocks.html: When two different fractions have conjugate denominators, there is a convenient common rational denominator. Work with each numerator as a whole before adding or subtracting.

blocks.title: Combine a simplified root and a rationalised fraction
blocks.prompt: Write \(\sqrt{48}+\frac{9}{\sqrt{3}}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\).
blocks.hint: Simplify the square root and give the fraction a rational denominator before combining.
blocks.solution:
The first term is \(4\sqrt{3}\) after extracting the square factor.

Multiply top and bottom of the fraction by \(\sqrt{3}\). It simplifies to \(3\sqrt{3}\). Add the coefficients.

The fully simplified result is \(7\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=7\).

blocks.html: A minus between fractions subtracts the second numerator in full. It changes every term in that numerator.

blocks.title: Rationalise a pair and combine
blocks.prompt: Write \(\frac{33}{6+\sqrt{3}}-\frac{33}{6-\sqrt{3}}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{3}\). Find \(a\).
blocks.hint: Rationalise each fraction with the other denominator. Keep the minus sign in front of the whole second result.
blocks.solution:
The denominators are conjugates. In each fraction, multiplying by the other denominator gives \(6^2-3=33\).

Cancel the numerical fraction in each term. Subtract the second full bracket using \(\left(6-\sqrt{3}\right)-\left(6+\sqrt{3}\right)\). The rational parts cancel.

The fully simplified result is \(-2\sqrt{3}\), so \(a=-2\).

examples.title: Choose a rationalising multiplier
examples.question:
Which multiplier makes \(4+2\sqrt{7}\) rational when used in a product?

  1. \(4-2\sqrt{7}\)
  2. \(2\sqrt{7}\)
  3. \(4+2\sqrt{7}\)
  4. \(4\)
solution: The product must have no surviving radical component. Use the bracket with the same rational part and the opposite radical part.
Multiplying by \(4-2\sqrt{7}\) gives \(4^2-4\times 7=-12\).

examples.title: Get an integer pair after rationalising
examples.question: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{3}{4+\sqrt{13}}\). Give the two integers \(a\) and \(b\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{13}\).
solution: Use \(4-\sqrt{13}\) as the common multiplier. Its radical term has the opposite sign.
The bottom becomes \(4^2-1\times 13=3\) after the cross terms cancel.
The top becomes \(12-3\sqrt{13}\). Simplify the signs and common factors to obtain \(4-\sqrt{13}\).

examples.title: Use a conjugate when the radical already has a coefficient
examples.question: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{52}{8+2\sqrt{3}}\). Give the two integers \(a\) and \(b\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{3}\).
solution: Use \(8-2\sqrt{3}\) as the common multiplier. Its radical term has the opposite sign.
The bottom becomes \(8^2-4\times 3=52\) after the cross terms cancel.
The top becomes \(416-104\sqrt{3}\). Simplify the signs and common factors to obtain \(8-2\sqrt{3}\).

examples.title: Make the final denominator positive
examples.question: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{2}{1-2\sqrt{13}}\). Give \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) in the form \(\frac{a+b\sqrt{13}}{c}\). Use integers with \(c>0\) and no common factor greater than 1.
solution: Use \(1+2\sqrt{13}\) as the common multiplier. Its radical term has the opposite sign.
The bottom becomes \(1^2-4\times 13=-51\) after the cross terms cancel.
The top becomes \(2+4\sqrt{13}\). Simplify the signs and common factors to obtain \(\frac{-2-4\sqrt{13}}{51}\).

examples.title: Combine a simplified root and a rationalised fraction
examples.question: Write \(\sqrt{99}+\frac{22}{\sqrt{11}}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{11}\). Find \(a\).
solution: The first term is \(3\sqrt{11}\) after extracting the square factor.
Multiply top and bottom of the fraction by \(\sqrt{11}\). It simplifies to \(2\sqrt{11}\). Add the coefficients.
The fully simplified result is \(5\sqrt{11}\), so \(a=5\).

examples.title: Rationalise a pair and combine
examples.question: Write \(\frac{14}{5+\sqrt{11}}-\frac{14}{5-\sqrt{11}}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{11}\). Find \(a\).
solution: The denominators are conjugates. In each fraction, multiplying by the other denominator gives \(5^2-11=14\).
Cancel the numerical fraction in each term. Subtract the second full bracket using \(\left(5-\sqrt{11}\right)-\left(5+\sqrt{11}\right)\). The rational parts cancel.
The fully simplified result is \(-2\sqrt{11}\), so \(a=-2\).

extraPractice.prompt: Which multiplier makes \(6+4\sqrt{3}\) rational when used in a product?
extraPractice.hint: Look for the bracket that gives a difference of two squares.
extraPractice.solution:
The product must have no surviving radical component. Use the bracket with the same rational part and the opposite radical part.

Multiplying by \(6-4\sqrt{3}\) gives \(6^2-16\times 3=-12\).

The bottom becomes \(6^2-1\times 7=29\) after the cross terms cancel.

The top becomes \(174-29\sqrt{7}\). Simplify the signs and common factors to obtain \(6-\sqrt{7}\).

extraPractice.title: Use a conjugate when the radical already has a coefficient

The bottom becomes \(10^2-16\times 2=68\) after the cross terms cancel.

The top becomes \(680-272\sqrt{2}\). Simplify the signs and common factors to obtain \(10-4\sqrt{2}\).

extraPractice.solution:
The denominators are conjugates. In each fraction, multiplying by the other denominator gives \(7^2-7=42\).

Cancel the numerical fraction in each term. Subtract the second full bracket using \(\left(7-\sqrt{7}\right)-\left(7+\sqrt{7}\right)\). The rational parts cancel.

The fully simplified result is \(-2\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=-2\).

glossary.definition: The bracket obtained by reversing the sign of the radical part in this chapter.
A product formed by pairing a rational term with a surd term.
An equal bottom value used to add or subtract fractions.
Having the same exact value.
Written in the requested form with square-free radicands and reduced numerical factors.

revision.body:
Use the conjugate

For \(a+b\sqrt d\), use \(a-b\sqrt d\). The cross terms cancel, and the denominator becomes \(a^2-b^2d\). Multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate preserves the exact value.

Handle signs and reduce a common factor

If the denominator is negative, move the negative sign through the entire numerator. Divide all integer coefficients and the denominator by their common factor before reading the requested values.

Choose the first useful step

When two different fractions have conjugate denominators, there is a convenient common rational denominator. Work with each numerator as a whole before adding or subtracting.

Example

For \(\frac{2}{1+\sqrt3}\), the conjugate is \(1-\sqrt3\). The denominator becomes \(-2\) and the fraction simplifies to \(\sqrt3-1\).

Check yourself

  • Give the conjugate of \(5-2\sqrt3\).
  • Rationalise \(\frac3{2+\sqrt5}\).

Answers \(5+2\sqrt3\) and \(-6+3\sqrt5\).
revision.checks:
• Multiplying by the root alone usually leaves a radical from the rational term. It cannot clear both terms.
  • In \(\frac{4-2\sqrt3}{-6}\), changing the denominator to 6 also changes both signs in the numerator. Cancelling requires a factor shared by both numerator terms and the denominator.
  • A minus between fractions subtracts the second numerator in full. It changes every term in that numerator.
